title: Refraction and Snell's law
goals: Say which way a wave bends when it slows down or speeds up at a boundary
Use Snell's law for light (refractive index) and for sound (velocities)
Work out a critical angle, and say when total internal reflection happens
Explain the first and second critical angles, and why angle probes send only shear waves
Work out the wedge angle an angle probe needs for a given beam angle in steel
summary:
When a wave crosses into a material where it travels at a different **speed**, it changes direction: **refraction**. Angles are measured from the **normal**, a line at right angles to the surface.

- Into a **slower** material, it bends **towards** the normal.
- Into a **faster** one, **away** from it.
- Hitting square on (along the normal), it goes straight through.

**Snell's law** for light uses the **refractive index** $n$ (how many times slower than in a vacuum): $n_1\sin\theta_1 = n_2\sin\theta_2$. For sound it is written with the speeds: $\frac{\sin\theta_1}{v_1} = \frac{\sin\theta_2}{v_2}$.

**Critical angle**: going into a faster material, there is an angle at which the refracted wave would skim along the surface (90°). Beyond it, nothing gets through: **total internal reflection** (TIR). $\sin\theta_c = \frac{v_1}{v_2}$ (or $\frac{n_2}{n_1}$ for light). Optical fibres trap light this way.

In solids, sound travels as **longitudinal** waves (L) and as slower **shear** waves (S, about 3240 m/s in steel against 5920 for L). A wave hitting a boundary at an angle makes both: **mode conversion**.

From a Perspex wedge (2730 m/s) into steel:

- **first critical angle** about **27.5°**: beyond it, no L wave in the steel
- **second critical angle** about **57°**: beyond it, no S wave either

Between them, only a shear wave enters: that is how **angle probes** work, with one clean beam (45°, 60°, 70° in steel). Wedge angle for a shear angle $\theta_s$: $\sin\theta_w = \sin\theta_s\frac{2730}{3240}$.

cards.q: Sound in a Perspex wedge (2730 m/s) meets a steel surface at 20° to the normal and carries on into the steel as a longitudinal wave (5920 m/s). In the steel, its angle to the normal is…
options: bigger than 20°
exactly 20°
smaller than 20°
0°: it goes straight down
cards.why: Steel is faster, so the wave bends away from the normal: the angle grows. (Snell's law gives about 48°.) Into a slower material it would bend towards the normal.

cards.title: Why waves bend
cards.body:
At a boundary between two materials, a wave's **speed** changes. Arriving at an angle, one side of the wavefront changes speed before the other, so the wave **turns**: **refraction**.

Angles are measured from the **normal**, a line at right angles to the surface.

- Into a **slower** material: bends **towards** the normal.
- Into a **faster** one: bends **away** from it.
- Square on (0°): no bend, just a speed change.
cards.more:
Picture a line of soldiers marching from a road onto mud at an angle. The ones who reach the mud first slow down while the others are still on the road, so the line swings round. Coming off the mud onto the road, the line swings the other way.

That is why a straw in a glass looks bent: light from the straw speeds up as it leaves the water and bends away from the normal on its way to your eye.

For sound in testing, steel is much faster than Perspex or water, so sound entering steel bends away from the normal, sharply.

cards.q: Light passes from air into water, where it is slower, at 40° to the normal. Which way does it bend?
options: Towards the normal: less than 40° in the water
Away from the normal: more than 40° in the water
It does not bend at all
It reflects back into the air
cards.why: Into a slower material, a wave bends towards the normal. Light is slower in water than in air.

cards.title: Snell's law for light
cards.body:
For light, each material has a **refractive index** $n$: how many times slower light is there than in a vacuum. Air is about 1.00, water 1.33, glass about 1.5.

$$n_1\sin\theta_1 = n_2\sin\theta_2$$

The **sine** of an angle is a number from 0 to 1 that grows with the angle (sin 30° = 0.5, sin 90° = 1): the calculator's sin key, in degrees. To get the angle back from its sine, use sin⁻¹.
cards.more:
Numbers: air into glass at 30°. $1.00 \times \sin 30° = 0.5$. In glass $1.5 \times \sin\theta_2 = 0.5$, so $\sin\theta_2 = 0.333$ and $\theta_2 = \sin^{-1} 0.333 = 19.5°$: bent towards the normal, as expected.

Why sines? The wavefront moves a distance proportional to its speed in each material in the same time, and the geometry of where it crosses the boundary turns those distances into sines of the angles. The details are in the trigonometry of a right-angled triangle; the result is that sines go in the ratio of the speeds.

cards.q: Light passes from air (n = 1.00) into glass (n = {ng}) at {a}° to the normal. At what angle to the normal does it travel in the glass?
cards.why: Snell's law: $1.00 \times \sin {a}° = {ng} \times \sin\theta_2$. Into the slower glass, the angle gets smaller.
cards.hint: Divide $\sin {a}°$ by the glass's index, then take sin⁻¹.

cards.title: Snell's law for sound
cards.body:
For sound, use the **speeds** directly:

$$\frac{\sin\theta_1}{v_1} = \frac{\sin\theta_2}{v_2}$$

So $\sin\theta_2 = \sin\theta_1 \times \frac{v_2}{v_1}$. Going into a material twice as fast, the sine doubles.

In ultrasonic testing: Perspex wedges about **2730 m/s**, water 1480, steel **5920** for longitudinal (L) waves and about **3240** for shear (S) waves.
cards.more:
It is the same law: refractive index is just 'how slow', so dividing by speed does the same job as multiplying by n.

Numbers: Perspex into steel (L) at 20°. $\sin 20° = 0.342$; times $\frac{5920}{2730} = 2.17$ gives 0.742; $\sin^{-1} 0.742 = 47.9°$. A 20° wedge makes a 48° beam: a large bend, because steel is more than twice as fast.

The immersion testing lesson used the same law for water into steel (four times as fast): a 5° tilt in water is about 20° in steel.

cards.q: A longitudinal wave in a Perspex wedge (2730 m/s) meets steel at {a}° to the normal. At what angle does the longitudinal wave travel in the steel (5920 m/s)?
cards.why: Into faster steel the sine grows by the speed ratio, so the angle grows a lot.

cards.title: The critical angle and total internal reflection
cards.body:
Going into a **faster** material, the refracted angle is always bigger than the incoming one. At the **critical angle** it reaches 90°: the wave would skim along the surface.

$$\sin\theta_c = \frac{v_1}{v_2}$$

(or $\frac{n_2}{n_1}$ for light, going from the higher index to the lower). Beyond the critical angle, none of it gets through: it all reflects back, **total internal reflection** (TIR). Optical fibres keep light inside by TIR.
cards.more:
Numbers: glass (1.5) to air (1.0): $\sin\theta_c = \frac{1.0}{1.5} = 0.667$, so 41.8°. Light inside the glass hitting the surface at more than 41.8° cannot get out.

An optical fibre is a thin glass core inside glass of slightly lower index: light travelling along it hits the boundary at a shallow, glancing angle, past the critical angle, and bounces along kilometres of fibre with almost no loss.

For sound, Perspex into steel (L): $\frac{2730}{5920} = 0.461$: 27.5°. Going the other way (into a slower material) there is no critical angle: it always gets through.

cards.q: Light inside a material of refractive index {n1} meets air (n = 1.00). What is the critical angle?
cards.why: At the critical angle the refracted ray is at 90°, and $\sin 90° = 1$: so $\sin\theta_c = \frac{n_2}{n_1}$.

cards.title: Two waves in steel: mode conversion
cards.body:
Solids carry sound two ways: **longitudinal** (L, compression, 5920 m/s in steel) and **shear** (S, side to side, about 3240 m/s). A wave meeting a boundary at an angle makes **both** in the steel, each at its own angle: **mode conversion**.

From a Perspex wedge (2730 m/s):

- below about **27.5°** (the **first critical angle**): both L and S enter, at different angles
- between 27.5° and about **57°** (the **second critical angle**): **only S** enters
- beyond 57°: nothing enters; it all reflects

Angle probes use the middle band: one clean shear beam.
cards.more:
Two beams at once would be confusing: an echo could come from either, at different angles and times. So angle probes are made with the wedge past the first critical angle, where the L wave is totally reflected and only the shear wave gets in.

The numbers: first critical, $\sin^{-1}\frac{2730}{5920} = 27.5°$; second critical, $\sin^{-1}\frac{2730}{3240} = 57.4°$.

Shear waves are slower, so they have a shorter wavelength at the same frequency: good for finding small flaws, and they cannot travel in liquids at all (liquids do not resist being sheared).

cards.q: Why is an angle probe's wedge set past the first critical angle?
options: So only a shear wave enters: one clean beam
So no sound at all enters the steel
So the longitudinal wave is twice as strong
So the probe can be used on liquids
cards.why: Past the first critical angle the longitudinal wave is totally reflected, leaving only the shear wave in the steel. One beam means each echo has one meaning.

cards.title: Working out a wedge angle
cards.body:
Probes are named by their **beam angle in steel** (45°, 60°, 70°, shear). The wedge needs a smaller angle in the Perspex. Turn Snell's law round:

$$\sin\theta_w = \sin\theta_s \times \frac{2730}{3240}$$

$\theta_w$ is the wedge angle, $\theta_s$ the shear angle wanted in steel. A 45° probe needs about **36.6°**; a 70° probe about **52°**. The marked angle is only right on steel (and a worn wedge changes it), so beam angles are checked on a calibration block.
cards.more:
Numbers: for 60° in steel. $\sin 60° = 0.866$; times $\frac{2730}{3240} = 0.843$ gives 0.730; $\sin^{-1} 0.730 = 46.9°$.

All the wedge angles land between the two critical angles (27.5° and 57.4°), as they must.

On aluminium (shear about 3100 m/s) the same 60° probe gives a slightly different angle: $\sin\theta = 0.730 \times \frac{3100}{2730} = 0.829$, so 56°. Probes are calibrated for steel; on other metals, check the angle.

cards.q: A shear-wave probe must give {s}° in steel (shear 3240 m/s) from a Perspex wedge (2730 m/s). What wedge angle?
cards.why: Snell's law the other way round: the slower wedge needs the smaller angle.

cards.q: What wedge angle gives a 45° shear wave in steel? (Perspex 2730 m/s, steel shear 3240 m/s.) Check it is between the critical angles.

steps.ask: Sine of the angle wanted in steel.
Times the speed ratio, wedge over steel.

steps.show: Yes: only the shear wave enters.

cards.why: Snell's law, solved for the first angle. The wedge is slower than steel's shear wave, so its angle is smaller.

cards.q: Why does step 2 multiply by 2730/3240 (less than 1), not 3240/2730?
cards.model: Snell's law says the sine of each angle divided by the speed in that material is the same. The wedge is the slower material, so its sine must be smaller in proportion: the steel sine times wedge speed over steel speed. Using the ratio upside down would give a sine bigger than the steel's, which would mean bending towards the normal on the way into a faster material: the wrong way.
points: sin θ ÷ v is the same both sides
The wedge is slower, so its sine is smaller
Upside down would bend the wrong way

cards.q: What wedge angle gives a 60° shear wave in steel?

steps.ask: Sine of 60°, times the speed ratio.

cards.why: Same steps; bigger beam angle, bigger wedge angle.

cards.q: What wedge angle gives a {s}° shear wave in steel (Perspex 2730 m/s, steel shear 3240 m/s)?
cards.why: Snell's law solved for the wedge angle.
cards.hint: Sine of the steel angle, times 2730/3240, then sin⁻¹.

cards.q: Sound passes from a wedge at {vw} m/s into steel. What is the second critical angle (where the shear wave, 3240 m/s, disappears)?
cards.why: The critical angle for the shear wave uses the shear speed: $\sin\theta_c = \frac{v_1}{v_S}$.

cards.q: Finding the angle in steel (L, 5920 m/s) from a 15° wedge (2730 m/s). One line is wrong. Which?
lines: So the beam bends towards the normal in the steel
cards.why: The ratio is upside down. Into faster steel the sine must grow, so multiply by fast over slow. The last line gives it away: a wave entering a faster material bends away from the normal, not towards it.

cards.q: What keeps light inside an optical fibre?
options: Total internal reflection at the core's boundary
A mirror coating on the outside
Refraction towards the normal
The fibre's plastic jacket absorbing stray light
cards.why: The core has a slightly higher index than the cladding round it, and light travels at glancing angles past the critical angle, so it reflects totally at every bounce.

cards.q: Light passes from water (n = 1.33) into air (n = 1.00) at {a}° to the normal. At what angle does it leave?
cards.why: Into the faster air, the sine grows by 1.33: it bends away from the normal. (Past about 48.8° it could not leave at all.)

cards.q: Is there a critical angle for sound going from steel into water?
options: No, some always gets through
Yes, at about 14.5° to the normal
Yes, at about 27.5° to the normal
Yes, at exactly 90° to the normal
cards.why: A critical angle only exists going into a faster material, where the refracted angle can reach 90°. Into slower water, the angle always shrinks, so some always refracts. (Water into steel has one: 14.5°.)

cards.q: A wave reflects off a boundary at 30° to the normal. At what angle does the reflected wave leave?
options: It depends on the two materials' speeds
cards.why: For reflection (same wave type, same material), the angle out equals the angle in. Snell's law is for the wave that crosses into the new material.

cards.q: An immersion probe is tilted {a}° in water (1480 m/s). What is the refracted shear-wave angle in steel (3240 m/s)?
cards.why: Same law, water as the first material and steel's shear speed as the second. Past 14.5° the longitudinal wave is gone, so this is the only beam.
cards.hint: Which two speeds: water and steel shear.

cards.q: Match each sum with the speeds it uses.
pairs: First critical angle, Perspex to steel
Second critical angle, Perspex to steel
Depth of a flaw from a 0° probe in steel
cards.why: Each rule needs the speeds of the wave types actually travelling: L for the first critical and 0° probes, S for the second critical.

cards.q: A wave passes from a fast material into a slow one at an angle. It bends…
options: towards the normal
away from the normal
not at all
straight back
cards.why: Slowing down, it bends towards the normal.

cards.q: First critical angle from Perspex (2730 m/s) into a metal with a longitudinal speed of {vm} m/s?
cards.why: Critical angle: sine equals slow over fast.

cards.q: Between the first and second critical angles, what enters the steel?
options: Only a shear wave
Only a longitudinal wave
Both kinds
Nothing
cards.why: Past the first critical angle the L wave is gone; before the second, the S wave still enters.
